title: Lipschitz and Holder conditions; constancy from a strong difference bound
section: Practice Test ▷ Question 38: a quantitative continuity condition
terms: Lipschitz continuity; Holder continuity; Holder exponent; uniform continuity; difference bound.

exposition.text:
A function on a subset of R is Lipschitz if |f(x) − f(y)| ≤ L|x − y| for one finite constant L
and every pair in its domain. More generally it is Holder continuous with exponent 0 < α ≤ 1
α
if |f(x) − f (y)| ≤ C|x − y| . Either bound implies uniform continuity. A bounded derivative
on an interval gives a Lipschitz bound by the mean-value theorem; the converse does not imply
differentiability everywhere, as |x| illustrates.
The practice question uses the stronger inequality with exponent 2. If an exponent α > 1 holds
on an interval, the function is constant. Indeed divide [x, y] into n equal pieces and add the
α 1−α
bounds to get |f(y) − f(x)| ≤ C|y − x| n → 0. This conclusion depends on being able to sub-
divide within the domain. On a disconnected domain, the function can have different constants
on different interval components, subject to the cross-component bounds. The terminology here
names the condition used in the question.
Uniform continuity means that for every ε > 0 one δ > 0 works for every pair of domain points:
|x − y| < δ implies |f(x) − f(y)| < ε. A Holder bound supplies δ from C, α, ε independently of
the points. Even a Lipschitz function can fail to be differentiable at a point, so these estimates
should not be used to assert existence of derivatives.

question.text:
2
Let E = [0, 1] ∪ [2, 3]. A function f : E → R satisfies f(0) = 0 and |f (x) − f(y)| ≤ (x − y) for all
x, y ∈ E. What is the largest possible value of f (3)?
(A) 0 (B) 1 (C) 2 (D) 4 (E) 9

solution.text:
The exponent-2 bound forces constancy on each interval, so f = 0 on [0, 1] and f = c on
[2, 3]. Taking x = 1, y = 2 gives |c| ≤ 1. The value c = 1 is attainable because points in
different intervals have distance at least 1; within each interval the difference is zero.

question.text:
A function on [0, 1] satisfies |f (x) − f(y)| ≤ |x − y|/ log(e/|x − y|) whenever x ̸= y. What must
be true?
(A) f is a nonconstant affine function.
(B) f must equal zero.
(C) f is strictly increasing.
(D) f is constant.
(E) f can be discontinuous.

solution.text:
Divide any interval [x, y] into n equal pieces. The triangle inequality bounds the total
change by (y − x)/ log(en/(y − x)), which tends to zero. Therefore f(x) = f(y) for every pair
of points.

question.text:
Suppose f is 2-Lipschitz and g is 3-Lipschitz, with the range of g contained in the domain of f.
What is the smallest universal Lipschitz bound for f ◦ g?
(A) 3 (B) 9 (C) 2 (D) 5 (E) 6

solution.text:
The inequalities give |f(g(x)) − f (g(y))| ≤ 2|g(x) − g(y)| ≤ 6|x − y|. Equality is attained by
f(t) = 2t and g(t) = 3t on R, so six is optimal.

question.text:
Let f(0) = 0 and f(x) = x sin(log x) for 0 < x ≤ 1. Which statement is correct?
(A) f is discontinuous at zero.
(B) f is Lipschitz on [0, 1] but has no right derivative at zero.
(C) f has right derivative zero at zero but is not uniformly continuous.
(D) f is uniformly continuous but cannot be Lipschitz.
(E) f is differentiable at zero with right derivative one.

solution.text:
′
The inequality |f(x)| ≤ x gives continuity at zero. For x > 0, f (x) = sin(log x) + cos(log x)
√
has absolute value at most 2. The mean-value theorem on any subinterval, including one
with endpoint zero, yields a Lipschitz bound. But [f (x) − f(0)]/x = sin(log x) oscillates
without a limit as x ↓ 0, so no right derivative exists.
